dedupe_keys.name: new york city network based access to emergency services and emergency service deserts

description: This case study measures transport access between emergency services and residents of New York City with a network-based method, identifying emergency service deserts where access to fire, emergency medical services, police and hospitals falls short of National Fire Protection Association guidelines. The authors, led by researchers at the US Army Engineer Research and Development Center, published it as a preprint. Travel times are routed on the road network from Emergency Services Sector sites to the community and related to site density and population density. Coverage is the five boroughs of New York City. The preprint is free to read and download on arXiv. Caveats: travel times are modelled from the road network, not observed response times, NFPA thresholds are used as the benchmark, and data sources are only summarised in the abstract. The study found that 95 percent of residents are well served but that Staten Island residents are disproportionately underserved, and discovered a negative power law between travel time and site density that policymakers could use to decide where new sites would help most. Simulation uses: quantifying the resilience of emergency service infrastructure by recomputing access when roads or sites are disrupted, and informing station location optimisation. Related records: NYC FDNY fire and EMS incident dispatch data (data-nyc-fdny-fire-incident-dispatch, data-nyc-fdny-ems-incident-dispatch) give observed response times for comparison.
